output.title: Why stopping rules are not enough in small-business workflows
output.body:
Stopping rules sound tidy until you meet the real workflow. In a small business, the issue is rarely the first rule. It is the exception: the invoice that is unusually large, the customer record that is incomplete, the lead that needs a human read, the file that does not fit the template. A simple if-then rule can stop work, but it can also stop the wrong work or let the wrong thing through.

So the useful question is not, “Can we write a rule?” It is, “Which judgment calls keep showing up in this repeated workflow?” If the answer is almost none, automation may not be worth the effort. If the answer is several, map the exceptions on one page. Mark what can be checked automatically, what should be flagged for review, and what must stay human-only.

That last part matters most where money is involved. Human approval stays in place for payments and other high-risk decisions. Bareni’s own accounts-payable demo showed amount-based human-only approval and refusal of agent approval or payment attempts, using synthetic data and a simulated blocked payment. Useful, not glamorous.

If your business already works in English, uses digital documents and SaaS tools, and has a frequent workflow with a measurable outcome, start there: one workflow, one exception map, one clear control point. The wrong rule is often more expensive than the manual step it was meant to replace.
